title: Strategy: pawn structure
blurb: Learn the weaknesses that pawns create (doubled and backward pawns), how to attack them with a pawn break, and then outposts, bishop versus knight, and active rooks.
deeperTitle: Bishop vs knight; outposts; rook activity

core.title: Pawns are the skeleton
body: Pawns cannot move backwards, so every pawn move changes the position for good. The **pawn structure** tells you where your pieces belong and where the weak points are.
Today: three weaknesses (doubled, backward and, from Day 8, isolated pawns) and how to attack them with a **pawn break**.

core.title: Doubled pawns
body: **Doubled pawns** are two pawns of the same colour on one file. They cannot protect each other, and the front one blocks the one behind.
Usually a weakness. Sometimes it is worth it: the half-open file helps your rooks.

board.caption: White’s pawns on c2 and c3 are doubled.

core.prompt: Tap a doubled pawn in Black’s position.
core.explain: The pawns on **f7** and **f6** share a file. Neither can protect the other, and Black’s kingside is weaker for it.

core.prompt: Take the knight. If Black takes back with the g-pawn, the f-pawns are doubled and the g-file is open. Then check with the queen.
core.hint: The bishop takes first, and after …gxf6 the queen can reach the open g-file.
core.explain: **Bxf6** takes the defender of the kingside. After **…gxf6** Black has doubled f-pawns and an open g-file, and **Qg4+** checks along it. Doubling the enemy’s pawns is a real gain, even without winning material.

core.title: Backward pawns
body: A **backward pawn** has fallen behind its neighbours, so no pawn can ever protect it, and the square in front of it is controlled by an enemy pawn.
It cannot move safely, and a rook on its file can attack it. The square in front is a hole for your pieces.

board.caption: Black’s d6 pawn is behind c5 and e5, and White’s e4 pawn controls d5.

core.explain: The pawn on **d6** is behind c5 and e5, and White’s e4 pawn controls d5. Nothing can protect it except pieces.

core.prompt: Black’s backward pawn on d6 is not defended by anything. Win it.
core.hint: Which of your pieces looks at d6 along an open file?
core.explain: The rook sees d6 down the open file, and nothing defends it. **Rxd6** wins a pawn. Backward pawns on open files are the first things to attack.

core.prompt: Black’s pawn structure has three kinds of weakness. Which pawn is **isolated** (no black pawn on a neighbouring file)?
core.explain: The pawn on **h7** has no black pawn on the g file, so no pawn can ever protect it. The pawns on f7 and f6 are doubled, and d6 is backward.

core.prompt: Which black pawns are **doubled** in the same position?
core.explain: **f7** and **f6** are on the same file. a7 and b7 are side by side, which is healthy, and c5 and d6 are on different files.

core.title: Pawn breaks
body: A **pawn break** is a pawn move that attacks an enemy pawn, to open lines or break up the enemy structure.
Break where the enemy is weakest, and where your pieces are ready to use the open lines.

board.caption: White’s c4 and e4 would both attack the pawn on d5.

core.prompt: White has two pawn breaks against the pawn on d5. Play one of them.
core.hint: A pawn move that attacks the pawn on d5.
core.explain: **c4** and **e4** both attack d5. **c4** keeps your pawn chain and opens the c-file; **e4** builds a big centre. Choose the one that fits your plan, and calculate what happens after Black takes.

core.prompt: Now you are Black. Black has two pawn breaks against the pawn on d4. Play one of them.
core.hint: A pawn move that attacks the pawn on d4.
core.explain: **…c5** and **…e5** both attack d4. The same idea from Black’s side: break where it opens lines for your pieces.

core.title: Hit the weak pawn
core.intro: Each position has a backward pawn on d6. Find the move that wins it.

puzzles.hint: A knight can take the pawn and attack two things at once.
puzzles.explain: **Nxd6** wins the backward pawn and forks the rook on e8 and the pawn on b7. After the rook moves, **Nxb7** wins a second pawn.

puzzles.hint: The pawn is attacked once and defended once. Add an attacker.
puzzles.explain: **Rd3** adds a second attacker on the backward pawn, and Black cannot hold it. Piling up on a weak pawn works when it cannot be defended enough.

puzzles.hint: You are Black. Which black pawn is backward?
puzzles.explain: The same idea from Black’s side: the rook takes the undefended backward pawn down the open file.

core.prompt: The enemy has a backward pawn. What is the best plan?
options: Put a rook on its file, and a piece on the square in front of it
Push your own pawns past it as fast as possible
core.explain: A backward pawn cannot move and cannot be protected by pawns, so attack it with rooks on its file, and plant a piece on the hole in front of it.

deeper.title: Outposts
body: An **outpost** is a square deep in the enemy half that **no enemy pawn can ever attack**, and that one of your pawns protects.
A knight there is very hard to remove. Here White’s d5 is an outpost: Black’s c and e pawns have already moved past it, so none can ever attack it.

board.caption: White’s pawn on e4 protects d5, and no black pawn can ever attack it.

deeper.prompt: Tap the outpost square for White’s knight.
deeper.explain: **d5** is protected by the pawns on c4 and e4, and Black has no pawn on the c or e file that could ever attack it.

deeper.prompt: Put your knight on the outpost.
deeper.explain: **Nd5** puts the knight where it cannot be chased by a pawn. From there it attacks b6, c7, e7 and f6.

deeper.prompt: How many squares does the knight on d5 attack?
deeper.explain: Eight, the most a knight can have. A knight in the centre is strong; on the edge it attacks far fewer squares.

deeper.prompt: Now you are Black. Put your knight on the outpost.
deeper.hint: The same idea from the other side of the board.
deeper.explain: **…Nd4** is the outpost: protected by the pawns on c5 and e5, and no white pawn can attack it.

deeper.title: Bishop or knight?
body: Bishops like **open** positions with long diagonals. Knights like **closed** positions and outposts, because they jump over pawns.
A knight on a strong outpost is often better than a bishop hemmed in by its own pawns. But in an open game with pawns on both wings, the bishop usually wins.

deeper.prompt: The centre is locked with pawns, and White has a safe outpost on d5. Which piece is usually better for White?
options: A knight, which can sit on the outpost
A bishop, because it is a long-range piece
deeper.explain: Closed position, outpost on d5: the knight is usually better. It jumps over the pawns and sits on a square that cannot be attacked by pawns.

deeper.title: Active rooks
body: Rooks are strongest on **open files** and on the **seventh rank**, where they attack the enemy pawns from behind.
A passive rook behind your own pawns does nothing. Look for the file nobody is using.

deeper.prompt: Which of White’s rooks attacks more squares?
options: The rook on d1, on the open file
The rook on a1, behind the pawn
deeper.explain: The rook on d1 attacks 13 squares, the one on a1 only 4. A rook behind its own pawns is passive. Put it on the open file.

deeper.prompt: Rooks belong on open files. Put one of your rooks on an open file.
deeper.explain: The c, d and e files are open, so any of these works. From an open file a rook can reach the other side of the board; on a closed file it is stuck behind its own pawns.

deeper.prompt: The d-file is open. Put your rook on the seventh rank, where it attacks two pawns.
deeper.hint: Up the open file as far as it goes.
deeper.explain: **Rd7** attacks b7 and f7 from behind. Black’s pieces are tied to defending them, and a rook on the seventh often wins pawns later.

puzzles.explain: The black pawns trap their own king.

puzzles.hint: Black can use the same trick against White.
puzzles.explain: White forgot to make luft, so the back rank falls.

puzzles.hint: The queen also travels along files.
puzzles.explain: A queen does the job of a rook here.
